lessonTitle: Welding, Brazing and Soldering: Processes and Weld Defects

blocks.text: A bracket weld looks perfect, with an even bead and no visible flaws, yet it parts at the first proof load. Cut open, the weld shows tiny gas pores along its length and a patch where the weld metal never fused to the plate. Knowing the process and what each defect means is what separates a joint that looks good from one that is good.

blocks.markdown: Joints can be classed by what happens to the parent metal (the pieces being joined). In **welding** the parent metal edges melt and fuse, usually with filler metal added, so the joint is made of the same family of metal. In **brazing** and **soldering** only a filler metal melts; the parent metal stays solid and the filler is drawn into the narrow gap by capillary action. The convention is that brazing filler melts above about 450 degrees C and soldering filler below it.

rows: Same or similar alloy, if any
Brass, silver or other alloy melting above about 450 degrees C
Tin-based alloys melting below about 450 degrees C
Above the parent melting point (steel about 1500 degrees C)
Low; used for sealing and electrical contact
Copper pipework, tool tips, dissimilar metals
blocks.caption: Typical values; exact temperatures depend on the alloys.

blocks.title: Arc welding
blocks.text: In arc welding an electric arc between an electrode and the work melts the joint edges and filler metal, forming a molten pool that solidifies into the weld. The pool must be protected from oxygen and nitrogen in the air by flux, slag or shielding gas, otherwise the weld becomes porous and brittle.

rows: Flux-coated consumable electrode; flux gives shielding gas and slag
Portable, outdoor site and repair work, structural steel
Continuous consumable wire fed through the gun, shielding gas supplied
Fast production welding of steel, aluminium, thin to thick sections
Non-consumable tungsten electrode, inert gas, filler rod added by hand
High-quality welds in thin sections, stainless steel, aluminium
Bare wire arc buried under a blanket of granular flux
High deposition on thick plate, long straight or circular seams
blocks.caption: Main arc welding processes.

blocks.markdown: The heat supplied to the weld affects its quality. The **heat input** per unit length of weld is the arc power times the efficiency, divided by the travel speed. Too much heat causes distortion and burn-through; too little causes poor fusion.

blocks.caption: Heat input per unit length H (J/mm) for arc efficiency eta, arc voltage V (V), welding current I (A) and travel speed v (mm/s).

blocks.title: Heat input
blocks.prompt: An arc weld uses 24 V, 200 A and travel speed 4 mm/s. The arc efficiency is 0.8. Find the heat input per millimetre of weld.

steps.text: Arc power: V x I = 24 x 200 = 4800 W.
Heat delivered to the work: multiply by the efficiency, 0.8 x 4800 = 3840 W.
Divide by travel speed: 3840/4 = 960 J per mm, or 0.96 kJ/mm.

blocks.answer: Heat input is 960 J/mm. Doubling the travel speed would halve it.

blocks.title: Filler metal for a fillet weld
blocks.prompt: A fillet weld has equal legs of 6 mm and a length of 400 mm. Treat the cross-section as a right triangle. Find the volume and the mass of weld metal (steel density 7.85 g/cm$^3$).

steps.text: Cross-section area of a triangle with both legs 6 mm: half of 6 x 6 = 18 mm^2.
Volume: area times length: 18 x 400 = 7200 mm^3 = 7.2 cm^3.
Mass: 7.2 x 7.85 = 56.5 g of deposited metal (more filler is needed to allow for losses such as spatter and stub ends).

blocks.answer: 7.2 cm^3 of weld metal, about 56.5 g.

blocks.markdown: **Weld defects.** Each defect has typical causes that point to the remedy. Learn the cause so that you change the right parameter rather than guessing.

rows: Contaminated plate (oil, rust, moisture), damp electrodes, loss of shielding gas, draughts, long arc
Weld metal not bonded to parent or to a previous pass
Current too low, travel too fast, poor torch angle, dirty surfaces
Current too low, root gap too small, speed too fast, wrong electrode size
Groove melted into parent beside the weld toe
Current too high, travel too fast, arc too long, wrong torch angle
Slag not cleaned between passes, wrong technique
Fracture in or beside the weld
High restraint, rapid cooling, hydrogen from damp flux, high carbon steel without preheat
Too much heat input, unbalanced welding sequence
blocks.caption: Common weld defects and their causes.

items: Clean the joint and keep electrodes dry to avoid porosity and hydrogen cracking.
Match current, voltage and travel speed to the plate thickness and joint.
Clean slag between passes in MMA and multi-pass welds.
Preheat thick or high-carbon steel and use a balanced welding sequence to control cracking and distortion.
Inspect visually, then by dye penetrant or radiography if the joint is critical.

blocks.title: Arc and fume hazards
blocks.text: The arc emits ultraviolet radiation that burns the eyes and skin, so a filter helmet and protective clothing are essential. Welding fume and shielding gas need extraction and ventilation, and hot spatter is a fire risk.

points: Welding melts the parent metal; brazing and soldering melt only a filler (above or below about 450 degrees C) that flows into the gap by capillary action.
MMA suits portable site work, MIG/MAG fast production welding, TIG high-quality thin sections and submerged arc thick plate with high deposition.
Defects such as porosity, lack of fusion, undercut, slag inclusions and cracking have characteristic causes, many linked to contamination, shielding and heat input.

questions.stem: A copper pipe fitting is joined using a filler alloy that melts at 650 degrees C without melting the copper, flowing into the joint by capillary action. What is this process?

distractorRationale.b: In welding the parent metal melts.
distractorRationale.c: Soldering uses a filler that melts below about 450 degrees C.
distractorRationale.d: Forge welding joins metals by heat and pressure without a molten filler.

questions.explanation: The parent copper stays solid while a filler melting above 450 degrees C wets the joint, which defines brazing. Soldering would use a filler melting below that temperature, and welding would melt the parent metal.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes soldering from welding?

options.text: In soldering only a low-melting filler melts and the parent metal stays solid
In soldering the parent metal melts, but in welding it does not
Soldering fillers melt above 900 degrees C
Soldering joints are stronger than welded joints

questions.correctOptionText: In soldering only a low-melting filler melts and the parent metal stays solid

distractorRationale.c: Solder melts at much lower temperatures, below about 450 degrees C.
distractorRationale.d: Soldered joints are weaker than welded ones.

questions.explanation: Soldering uses a filler that melts below about 450 degrees C and does not melt the parent metal. Welding melts the parent edges as well and gives a much stronger joint.

questions.stem: A fabricator must weld thin stainless steel tube with a clean, precise, high-quality bead and add filler by hand only where needed. Which arc process best fits?

distractorRationale.b: Submerged arc suits thick plate and long straight seams.
distractorRationale.c: MMA is less precise and leaves slag, so it suits site work more than thin tubes.
distractorRationale.d: Oxy-fuel cutting is not a joining process.

questions.explanation: TIG uses a non-consumable tungsten electrode and inert gas, with filler added separately, giving fine control for thin sections and stainless steel. Submerged arc and MMA are used for thicker or site work.

questions.stem: A maintenance welder must repair a steel frame outdoors, away from mains-gas supplies, with portable equipment. Which process is most suitable?

distractorRationale.b: Outdoor draughts blow away TIG's shielding gas and it needs gas cylinders.
distractorRationale.c: Submerged arc requires a flat, fixed set-up and large equipment.
distractorRationale.d: MIG without shielding gas gives porous welds.

questions.explanation: The flux-coated electrode in MMA generates its own shielding, and the equipment is simple and portable. Gas-shielded processes are disturbed by wind.

questions.stem: A weld shows scattered small round gas pores through its length. Which cause is most likely?

options.text: Contaminated or damp plate or electrodes, or loss of shielding gas
Slag not cleaned from the previous pass
Welding current too high, giving a groove at the toe

questions.correctOptionText: Contaminated or damp plate or electrodes, or loss of shielding gas

distractorRationale.b: Slag not cleaned causes slag inclusions, not pores.
distractorRationale.d: Too small a gap gives incomplete penetration.

questions.explanation: Porosity is caused by gas trapped in the solidifying pool, from moisture, oil or rust or from a failed shield. The other options correspond to different defects.

questions.stem: An arc weld uses 22 V and 180 A at a travel speed of 5 mm/s, with an arc efficiency of 0.8. What is the heat input in J/mm?
questions.explanation: The arc power is $22\times180=3960$ W. Applying the efficiency gives 3168 W, and dividing by 5 mm/s gives 633.6 J/mm.

questions.stem: A fillet weld has equal legs of 8 mm and a length of 250 mm, with a triangular cross-section. What is the volume of weld metal in cm$^3$?
questions.explanation: The cross-section area is $0.5\times8\times8=32$ mm^2. The volume is $32\times250=8000$ mm^3, which is 8.0 cm^3.

questions.stem: The fillet weld above (8.0 cm$^3$ of weld metal) is deposited in steel of density 7.85 g/cm$^3$. What is the mass of deposited metal in grams?
questions.explanation: The mass is volume times density, $8.0\times7.85=62.8$ g. Extra filler is purchased to cover spatter and stub-end losses.

questions.stem: Distinguish welding, brazing and soldering in terms of what melts and the strength of the joint, and give an application for each.
markingGuide: Welding: parent metal melts and fuses, strongest joint, structures or pressure vessels
Brazing: only filler melts, above about 450 degrees C, flows by capillary action, strong joint, e.g. copper pipework or tool tips
Soldering: filler melts below about 450 degrees C, parent metal stays solid, weakest, electronics or sealing
Capillary action or narrow gap fit for brazing and soldering
Relative strength ranking welding > brazing > soldering
questions.explanation: The defining difference is whether the parent metal melts and, for filler-only joints, the filler's melting temperature relative to 450 degrees C. Strength and application follow from that difference.

questions.stem: An inspector finds three defects in a weld: undercut along the toes, slag inclusions between passes and cracking in a thick high-carbon plate. State a likely cause and a remedy for each defect.
markingGuide: Undercut: current too high, travel too fast or arc too long; reduce current or speed, correct torch angle
Slag inclusions: slag not removed between passes; clean thoroughly and adjust technique
Cracking: high restraint, rapid cooling, hydrogen or high carbon content
Remedy for cracking: preheat, low-hydrogen consumables and a suitable welding sequence
Links each cause to a process parameter or practice
questions.explanation: Each defect points to a particular parameter or practice, so the remedy is targeted. Cracking in a thick high-carbon plate needs control of cooling rate and hydrogen, not just a change of current.
